title: The ghettos
hook: Jews are forced into walled, crowded, starving districts of occupied cities

segments.voice: Yesterday, closed doors, and your line: doors closed. Today the war has begun, and for the Jews of occupied Poland there is no door out. Go gently.

A notice is pasted on a wall in a city in occupied Poland. All Jews must move, by a set date, into a few named streets. Families load carts with whatever they can push: a table, bedding, a sewing machine, the good dishes. Behind them they leave homes they have lived in for years. Ahead of them, workers are building a wall. When it's finished, there will be guards at the gates, and the streets inside will hold far more people than they were ever built for.
screen: `A NOTICE ON THE WALL.` → `CARTS FULL OF WHAT THEY COULD CARRY.` → `A WALL GOING UP.`

segments.voice: After the German army occupied Poland and other lands to the east, Jews in city after city were forced into ghettos: sealed districts, closed off by walls or wire, in places like Warsaw and Lodz. Several families shared a single room. Jews had to wear a badge or an armband. Food was rationed on purpose, far below what a body needs. Hunger came first, then disease, and people began to die in the streets. And still, inside the walls, people organized life. House committees ran soup kitchens. Doctors treated the sick with almost nothing. Teachers held classes. Some children squeezed through gaps in the wall to smuggle food back to their families, risking their lives for a few potatoes. Many ghettos had a Jewish council, forced by the Germans to carry out their orders, and people argued then, and historians still argue, about the impossible choices those councils faced. People inside could not know the ghettos were a stage on the way to something worse. The Torah has a line about hunger, spoken by Moses as he recalls the manna in the wilderness: "Man doth not live by bread only." It does not say bread doesn't matter; in the wilderness, God gave bread. It says a person needs bread and something more. In the ghettos people starved for bread, and also for dignity, for learning, for each other, and they kept feeding that second hunger even when the first could not be fed. Jews bless God before eating bread, thanking God for bringing bread out of the earth. In the ghetto, some said that blessing over almost nothing.
screen: `SEALED DISTRICTS, WALLS AND WIRE.` · `HUNGER, THEN DISEASE.` · `SOUP KITCHENS, CLASSES, SMUGGLERS.` · `BREAD, AND SOMETHING MORE.` · then, large: `MAN DOTH NOT LIVE BY BREAD ONLY.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the next thing you'll eat, and see it plainly, noticing what it took to reach you. Let the people of the ghettos come near, without forcing any picture. If you pray, you can say the blessing your tradition uses before eating; if you don't, one quiet breath is enough.
The ghettos. The sealed, crowded, starving districts where Jews in occupied cities were forced to live, and where they still ran soup kitchens and schools. Today's word.
Your line: almost nothing to bless. Inside the walls, they fed the second hunger too. Go gently.

howItsDone: Jews say a blessing before eating, over bread thanking God for bringing bread out of the earth, and some families remember the ghettos at Holocaust memorial gatherings with readings of diaries and testimonies written there.

chat.says: What was life like inside the ghettos? Did people just give up?
options: Hunger and disease were terrible, yet people ran soup kitchens, classes and care.
Food was scarce, but the ghettos were mostly safe places to wait out the war.
People gave up hope, and no one tried to keep schools or kitchens going.
